planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant out only after soil and nights have warmed, since this slender hot pepper sulks in cool ground.

directions: Baklouti is the slim, fiery pepper long grown around Tunisia's Cap Bon peninsula and Nabeul region, where it forms the backbone of true Tunisian harissa paste. Plants are compact and heavily branched, setting clusters of thin pods that are picked both green and ripe red and typically sun-dried or fire-roasted before grinding. Give it a long warm season, steady even moisture, and full sun, and harvest continually to keep pods coming through summer. It is prized for a bright, fruity heat distinct from the smokier ancho-type chiles used in other regional pastes.
sources: INRAT (Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique de Tunisie)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked; this landrace is biennial and overwinters outdoors even under salt-laden Shetland gales, so it can also be sown in late summer for winter and spring greens.

directions: Shetland Kale is a non-heading, loose-leaved brassica landrace kept for generations in crofts on Scotland's Shetland Islands, bred by nothing more than isolation and salt wind into one of the hardiest kales grown anywhere. It does not form a tight head like modern cabbage but instead produces an open rosette of blue-green leaves that are picked individually and cooked like collards or kale. It tolerates thin, wind-scoured soils and brief seawater spray better than most brassicas, making it a useful choice for coastal or exposed cool-climate gardens. Seed is maintained mainly through UK heritage seed networks and genebank collections rather than mainstream catalogs.
sources: University of Warwick Vegetable Genetic Resources Unit

planting.note: Wait until soil is thoroughly warm after last frost before direct sowing, since this long-season Central Asian melon needs consistent heat to fill out its thick keeping rind.

directions: Zard Kampir, whose Uzbek name translates roughly as 'old woman,' is a traditional Fergana Valley melon famous not for eating fresh off the vine but for keeping: its thick rind lets whole melons hang in cool storerooms for months, often brought out for winter and New Year gatherings. The vines sprawl widely and want a long hot continental-style summer and deep, infrequent watering rather than frequent shallow irrigation, which mimics the arid conditions it was selected under. Flesh is firm, pale, and only moderately sweet when first picked, developing fuller flavor and softness after weeks of storage. It is a good choice for gardeners wanting a genuinely different melon-keeping tradition from the quick-eating cantaloupes common in Western gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past last frost; this melon fruits fast for a Central Asian type but still needs sustained summer heat to turn properly sweet.

directions: Amal is a traditional Uzbek melon grown through the hot, dry continental summers of the Samarkand and Fergana regions, where it is picked and eaten fresh at the height of ripeness rather than stored like some of its longer-keeping Central Asian relatives. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, rewarding full sun and deep, widely spaced watering over frequent shallow irrigation. The orange flesh is intensely aromatic and sweet, reflecting the strong sugar accumulation Central Asian melons develop under long, hot, low-humidity growing seasons. It makes a good warm-climate alternative to Western cantaloupe types for gardeners wanting a more fragrant, old-world melon flavor.

planting.note: Give it plenty of room and wait for reliably warm soil after last frost, since Gulyabi makes large sprawling vines and needs a long hot season to size up.

directions: Gulyabi is a large oblong melon landrace traditionally grown around Tashkent and through the Fergana Valley, where its musky, aromatic flesh is eaten fresh in season and also sliced into long strips and sun-dried into a chewy winter treat called qoqi. The vines grow larger than most Western melon varieties and respond best to deep, infrequent watering rather than frequent light irrigation, echoing the arid conditions of its home region. It needs a genuinely long, hot summer to mature fully, making it best suited to warm continental or desert-adjacent climates. Its distinctive perfume and dense sweetness set it apart from the milder cantaloupes typically found in American gardens.
